A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Memory-R1. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures and algorithms, are readable and support reliable comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies can be identified without treating them as missing material.

before.justification: v1 reports original LoCoMo evaluations, component ablations, training curves and agent behavior case studies.

after.justification: v4 retains original evaluations and adds supervised-baseline, model-scale, cross-dataset and reward-design results.

M1.justification: The two-agent architecture, operation set, memory distillation and PPO/GRPO objectives remain. The published construction pseudocode locally changes UPDATE/DELETE from editing an individual m_j in v1 Algorithm 1 to merging/removing the retrieved set M_ret in v4 Algorithm 3. Removing Appendix B's operation-label language clarifies the RL approach already described in v1; it does not establish a new training regime.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from LoCoMo alone to modified MSC and the oracle version of LongMemEval. These add distinct conversational data and evaluation requirements involving preferences, knowledge updates and multi-session information integration. Training remains confined to LoCoMo.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes LangMem and adds Memory-SFT for both backbones. Memory-SFT uses the same architecture and training data with behavior cloning from GPT-5 trajectories, introducing an important supervised-versus-RL control. LoCoMo, Zep, A-Mem and Mem0 remain; renaming LoCoMo to LoCoMo (RAG) does not introduce another comparator.

E3.justification: v4 introduces transfer evaluation without additional training on modified MSC and LongMemEval-oracle, and adds Qwen 3B/14B configurations. The LoCoMo split, metrics and principal decoding settings remain. Appendix B changes the stated memory-history window from 50 to 24 turns, but v4 Algorithm 1 still specifies 50; this is a reported setting revision with unresolved implementation.

E4.justification: New analyses test cross-dataset transfer, model-size sensitivity and Judge-based versus exact-match rewards. Figure 5 also adds PPO without memory distillation, whereas v1 Table 4 reports that comparison only for GRPO. The original component ablations, stronger-manager comparison, training curves and Appendix A case studies are retained, often reformatted.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.1 states that every configuration is evaluated three times and mean scores are reported. v4 omits this statement while retaining surrounding settings in Appendix D, and supplies no replacement repeat-count or uncertainty-reporting practice. This establishes reduced reporting, not that fewer evaluations were performed.

E6.justification: All shared Table 1 rows retain identical numbers; LangMem results are removed and Memory-SFT results added. v4 additionally reports model-scale, MSC, LongMemEval and reward-comparison outcomes. These include mixed findings: LongMemEval Qwen Judge scores are 53.2 for BASE, 47.4 for PPO and 57.8 for GRPO. Appendix Table 3 also gives Qwen-7B results differing from retained Table 1 without clearly distinguishing conditions, preventing a same-setting version-performance interpretation.

T1.justification: The policy, PPO/GRPO objective, group-relative advantage and exact-match reward definitions remain mathematically equivalent. Moving the advantage formula into prose and renumbering equations do not change theory. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion expand the generalization claim to three named benchmarks, 3B–14B model scales and transfer without retraining. The central contributions—two-agent RL memory management, data efficiency with 152 training examples and strong LoCoMo performance—remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds a substantive explanation that Judge-based rewards encourage verbose answers and conflict with string-overlap metrics. New limitations identify dialogue-focused evaluation, untested multimodal applicability and the complexity of separately training the agents. Existing interpretations of memory consolidation, filtering and stronger upstream memory are largely retained.

D1.justification: v4 newly names VERL, specifies eight H100 GPUs for the 14B model, adds training pseudocode and expands explanations of staged training and frozen components. It also documents dataset licensing and segmentation. Most existing hyperparameters and prompt contents are retained or relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: The introduction adds Tensor Brain and traces memory operations through database CRUD, MemLLM and AIOS, explicitly attributing the adopted operator set to Mem0. New benchmark and implementation references appear, while LangMem and several general agent references disappear. v1's characterization of A-Mem as RL-based is removed, but the main RL-memory novelty positioning remains.

P1.justification: Much of the main text is rewritten and condensed. The pipeline overview is integrated into Section 3, implementation details move into Appendix D, and dataset documentation is reorganized into testing and training subsections. The evaluation narrative gains a generalization section, with separate limitations and extended-results sections.

P2.justification: v1's three ablation tables are reorganized into v4's four-panel Figure 5. New scaling and transfer plots, a reward-comparison table and extended-results tables substantially change the evidence presentation. Existing plots and algorithms are relocated, prompt displays gain shaded boxes, and the document is extensively reflowed.

improvement.justification: The supervised control, reward-design comparison and transfer evaluations make v4's empirical case more informative than v1's single-benchmark study, while explicit limitations improve qualification. These benefits are tempered by conflicting 24/50-turn settings, loss of three-evaluation reporting, and broad improvement claims contradicted by some Judge results in Appendix F. The added diagnostic evidence supports a limited net quality gain.
